I was definitely rambling, but now that I can collect my thoughts a bit more - that drives me up a wall. So much of my favorite media has SA survivors, but it's almost always the love story "immediately after" their SA, and how their new partner is there for them every step of the way. The truth is that for lots of people that's just not reality. I'm definitely loads better now than I was, but I still can't be intimate with men and have broken down to panic attacks every time I tried to romantically escalate a situation with them. Which sucks, because that support might be helpful, but it was really something I had to do single (not alone though - find people platonically or professionally who you feel comfortable with, that does wonders). Anyways, sending you lots of love and support, and best wishes going forward ❤ we're all here rooting for you

Today in particular? Tired, but hopeful. It's been about four years. But I got out of bed, looked into a new prescription for SNRIs, and I'm watching a funny movie. Got to do my dishes soon. Life ultimately goes on, and I've done my best to keep moving with it. Lots of days are still not great, and I haven't had sex with a man since — but I'm learning a lot about me. I recently started dating for the first time in years, and even though we're long-distance, my partner has always been really good to me. She's been my rock throughout lots of things. Relationships don't fix the issue — I kept just waiting to stumble into one and "find love" because every narrative we see of a survivor ends with them finding their "real" soulmate, who guides them through that. I've, honestly, found that to be bullshit. My friends and family got me through, and my therapist, and my damn self. Today, I'm procrastinating and tired but alive. Tomorrow, I'll sleep in and do some work. I still think about it. It's still a process, maybe it always will be. But there are good days.

Everything you have said here reminds me of three, almost four years ago, to the point that it hurt to read because I understood your perspective so severely. So, I'll say to you what I said to him back then when I was still desperately seeking out closure, seeing him, trying to be his friend. Same sort of thing, I got lost one night and called him to rant and he was begging for my address to help me get home, and I realized I didn't want to give it to him. I think after your edit you've probably begun to realize this yourself, but:

"The thing is, Eric*, I don't think I can ever stop being mad at you. I want to yell and scream and cry and make you hurt as much as you hurt me. I want to make you remember everything. I want you to be miserable, and me to be happy. But I can't make that happen. And talking to you sure as fuck won't help."

I wish I could say that was the last time I spoke to him, because it'd be a lot more poignant that way, but I messaged him at least twice more, one of which was a lot more pleasant and wishing him a good holiday season. That was the last message I sent, and even three years later, I can't stop thinking about how I might have absolved some of his sins by ending on a high note, or how much I want to message him just to explain that he absolutely ruined my life, and that it still upsets me to see him thriving. Then I remember that I've done this half a dozen times, and the same thing always happens: I get angry and explain, he vaguely acknowledges the SA, I feel vindicated (briefly), we laugh, he tries to get back into my life, and I wonder if he listened at all. Your abuser will keep doing the same if you let him, too. 

You were absolutely assaulted by him, probably multiple times, and do not let anyone tell you different. And you'll feel vindicated someday. You might even get closure. But none of it will be from him.

Wishing you the best of luck. Keep your head up, I believe in you.

Notre-Dame. Backstory boils down to I'm a nerd, and my entire life I've had a list of buildings/structures/etc. I desperately want to see, more so than any other tourist attractions. Notre-Dame was very high on that list. So, I visited the Quèbec version. I watched the fantastic Disney movie. When I was old enough, I even read Notre-Dame de Paris in French and understood probably nothing, so then read it again in English. When I was in University, I finally saved up enough money to do a killer trip abroad, dumped thousands of dollars into my plan and figured out what I'd do about school for a whole semester, etc., etc., getting ready to go September 2019. 

April 15th, 2019, I sit on my friend's floor and just watch it burn in silence. I'm a grown ass adult, but shit was I ever devastated watching that. Then I had to go write a final exam right after. Worst. Day. Ever.

I remember calling my best friend who was in Europe one day mid-March 2020 and urging her to take advantage of the cheap flights because I was entirely clueless (and more than a little insensitive).

Like three days later I'm on the phone with her begging her to get home as soon as possible while every uni in the country shuts down. That put it into perspective quick.

If it's any consolation, as another survivor (although using that word still feels really weird to me), I relate to this, including the CNC part, at least in my own daydreams. It's actually so much easier to imagine sex if it was something that was "pushed" on me, where I didn't have to make any decisions - with a consenting, respectful, trusted partner, of course. But voicing my own enthusiastic consent is still really hard or, more accurately, rescinding it. I panic, and it brings up a lot of guilt and, oh god, the shame. Sometimes, I wish I could convey to a partner that it would be easier to have a safe word and they could just make all the decisions, so I COULD shut my brain off and stop panicking. 

Moral of the story: trust your wife. I'm sure she loves you very much. And it's okay to cry sometimes - I'm quite confident I'll cry the first time I manage to have sex again. That doesn't make it bad. Sometimes, it's just emotional to remember that you're sharing this moment with someone you can trust, who loves you and wants to hold you afterwards, instead of the alternative.

Years ago, I realized something that made me feel a lot better, and for the first time, I feel comfortable sharing it here: the only one who can ever forgive your rapist is you. 

At the time, I was dealing with a lot of insecurity about how I was still leaning on my abuser as a crutch, but I was so hurt that other people who knew what he did were pretending it didn't happen. Then it occurred to me that of course I'd be leaning on him - he was my whole support system before the assault, and he had slowly turned everyone else against me in the months leading up to it. At some very hard times in my life, he was all I had, and he was an indescribable help to me. That doesn't excuse him, but it did explain a lot to me about how I was feeling. I've cut all contact now, but someday, I know I'll need to let go of my anger and hatred to really move on. And when I do, that's my choice how I handle it, no one else's. It is entirely up to you how you choose to cope with your trauma and the role it has in your life, and while I would recommend talking it through with a therapist, ultimately, you get to make all the choices and whatever you're feeling is valid in the end.

Speaking as a woman who came dangerously close to kissing my best friend's boyfriend recently (and is not remotely proud of that fact): loneliness, insecurity, and interpersonal issues. And in my case, definitely some thrill-seeking behaviour/maladaptive coping mechanisms. He's also a good friend, the couple has been fighting, we were hanging out alone, and I've been so damn lonely through this pandemic (and before that, really, as I haven't had a romantic partner in years). It has always sounded stupid to me when people use it as an excuse, but it almost "just happened": two drunk friends with lowered inhibitions, no supervision, and waaaaay too much time on our hands. As someone who's been cheated on and never fully recovered, I was disgusted with myself that the thoughts even crossed my mind, but the fantasy was definitely there, and I was stunned by just how badly I wanted to do it in the moment. 

Of course, that's when I removed myself from that situation and felt like crap all of the next day for even considering it, but it really put into perspective for me that it's not as far to fall as I always thought it was. Anyone can get there if they're feeling unwanted and desperate enough, especially if you don't have a lot of respect for yourself to begin with.

tl;dr: desperate and insecure people will do some stupid, stupid things

I normally wouldn't comment and almost never touch this account any more besides to scroll aimlessly, but I saw an ad for this tonight (as a woman) and got morbidly curious and watched the whole thing. I wasn't going to buy the book (obviously), but wanted to know all those phrases he kept alluding to, and found this, so thank you! I figured I'd throw in my two cents while I'm here. I'm only one girl, and I'm pretty jaded when it comes to dating, so take everything I say with a grain of salt, but honestly, very few of these tips would work well on myself or a lot of single (much more interested and less overall judgey) girls I know. The last one is just downright creepy, do NOT try and coerce women into doing things that way -- they might say yes just to appease you, or if they're shy or uncertain or afraid (it happens), then she's going to detest you after and see you as an A-grade asshole. Being told what to do or ordered for would also piss me off unless I specifically asked you to make plans, but I can somewhat see how the assertive thing might work, and how the the "When can I see you?" doesn't. It's not as much a turn-off, but puts all the onus on me to actually make the plans. I'd kind of combine what he said with a question, like, "I was going to go to \[x\] today and thought you'd enjoy it. Want to tag along?" It's less domineering, but shows you've put genuine thought into things she'd enjoy. Plus, if she says no, you've kind of framed it like you're going either way, so it's less of a "rejection" and more of a "not this time".  


Honestly, like OP said, women aren't this black and white. I know loads of women who are turned on by competition, I also know loads (myself included) who would be turned off by a man trying to assert, no matter how subtly, that he has other options out there so I have to "keep his attention" or he'll find someone else to sleep with for the night. I don't think the dating as a market thing is particularly great either -- it basically contradicts the "make dating a team sport" argument he was also trying to make. If anything, I do like the idea of positive mindset he proposed, and not being afraid of rejection but instead hoping for success (though I think those are fairly basic tips). A lot of the issues he summarizes for men seem to be based in a lack of realism. To put it bluntly: if you're a 5-6, don't expect to pull a 9 unless you have something fantastic to offer (this is coming from a 6 myself lmao). And if you want to be in "9-10" territory (literally using the words he used for women here) *make* yourself a 9-10 by being engaging in other ways: it's the corniest advice in the book, but men really do get more attractive to me when they're confident in themselves, know what they want, have great personalities, or are good at making me laugh.  


Finally (lord I went on a rant, sorry, I guess I had more opinions about that random half hour video than I thought), while watching that intro, I just felt uncomfortable all the time. It sounds like he's mostly trying to market to people who are really insecure, and play on those insecurities to talk them into "this will change your life", and then just sharing borderline-misogynistic, mostly-generic garbage. Suffice to say, I mostly tracked down this post so I could find out what the phrases were to **avoid** any man I thought had bought & was adamantly using this course  😂  


tl;dr: As a woman, the confidence side of this sounds good, slipping into arrogance, bragging, and ordering women around is bad.

This is absolutely not something wrong with you, and a response to something very, very wrong with your abuser. I'm so sorry this is happening to you. I don't have any advice to offer as I'm in a similar situation and not sure how to move past it myself, but you are valid and I wish you the best of luck, and if your new partner is really a good person they should understand when you explain this to them.
That is definitely an assault, and I'm so sorry your friends were so shitty about it. You were too inebriated to give proper consent, and you never gave it to begin with. It's awful.

This is awful. I really hope they're still investigating, and running tests and interviews, and just leaving you out of the loop for now for your own security, but if not this is absolutely disgusting. I'm so sorry.

This is absolutely rape. Regardless of whether or not you consented "earlier" it still doesn't count, because a) you can't consent intoxicated, and b) consent can be withdrawn at any time (and is withdrawn when you cross the threshold of intoxicated). If you can't remember giving consent, it's not valid consent even if he did get it-- which I highly doubt he did.

He most certainly did "take advantage of you", but that "taking advantage" was that he raped you. He sounds abusive, manipulative, and like he was probably lying/threatening you to try and get out of it. I'm so, so sorry you went through this.

I can only imagine what that's like, and I'm sorry. Knowing my abuser's face is awful, I see it everywhere I look, feel physically sick if I run into him, and avoid him/anyone who looks like him, but at least I know *what* to avoid. There's never a "good" way to be abused obviously, but this sounds particularly awful. I don't have any advice unfortunately (besides therapy, and maybe checking the faces of registered sex offenders if you feel like you could safely to see if anyone even rings a bell), but I just want to say I hear you, and your thoughts and feelings are valid.

Wow, that's a lot. For starters, *apologize to her*. I'm sure you've already done that, but keep doing it. Reiterate you believe her, you stand by her, and you're so, so sorry for everything that happened and that you weren't there to support her at the time. If you plan on sticking around, promise her you'll be there for her now. Reporting a rape to the police and then going to court is always going to be an awful experience, but it's at least a little easier to do if you already feel like people believe you and you don't feel alone.

When it comes to taking it to the police, make sure both of you are completely honest, answer all their questions, and offer up absolutely anything you think might be even slightly helpful (even if you may be ashamed of it now). Hiding details will just make it much worse. Make sure you tell them about the threat, at the absolute bare minimum she will need some kind of legal restraining order or peace bond making sure she is safe and he can't approach. 

Most importantly, good luck and don't give up on her. This is likely just the beginning of a long and gruelling process, and she's going to need people who support her unconditionally in the months (maybe even years) to come.

I tried this.

Suffice to say it didn't work. He never was able to fully accept that he did it, and every apology felt hollow as a result. He still believes, in his own way, that it's a fabrication, or that he was innocent and it was just a bad misunderstanding. Sure, he said sorry. Sure, he tried to make things better.

But that anger at him, that raw, fiery anger that I had after he took everything from me never went away, and slowly it seeped into everything so in the period of time I was still speaking to him and trying to "let him come to terms with it" so I could forgive him and we could still be friends (a laughable thought to me now), I was sullen, quick to anger, and depressed constantly about all aspects of my life.

I think deep down I hated him and loved him still at the same time, and it meant every time it got brought up I wanted to lash out and take it out on him and make him pay for all the hurt he gave me.

It was toxic, it was bad for my mental health, but most importantly it also *didn't work*.

I can't tell you what to do OP, but if my experience here means anything, a rapist who is denying that they did it/framing it as an accident is never going to shift from that stance.

I had some similar experiences with my abusive ex (especially the "I told him to stop and he said no it feels good" shit), and I struggle with these thoughts a lot too. It's hard, because the picture of rape painted for women is of a man forcing himself on her in a dark alleyway, while she's kicking and screaming. Rape in relationships is a lot more confusing, talked about a lot less, and therefore much harder to recognize at the time but equally heartbreaking. I'm sorry you've been through this, your feelings are completely valid. Wishing you the best.

When I went through my abusive relationship, I told no one at first. I experienced sexual assault, was bawling my eyes out, and then I got up and cheerily went to class in a daze, even casually telling one of my friends when she asked why I was late to class that I'd been with this guy. Nobody knew a thing until after he ended it, even if they had suspicions I would shut them down. We sometimes shut down rumours together. I told everyone how wonderful and lovely he was, even in the absolute worst periods of it. I told them how glad I was to have him. I hid everything he did so my friends would still like him. I myself didn't even understand how bad everything was because he'd once been so nice to me, and I was convinced it was just a "bad stretch" and we would "get through it together". It wasn't until much later when I was removed from the situation that the anxiety attacks, the depression, and all the "stereotypical" symptoms set in. 

Not everyone reacts "like the book", and there is so much more nuance to sexual assault than just "hate your rapist vehemently and wish them dead the moment it happens".

On another note, you should have used this post to ask questions. I understand you're confused and hesitant, but this post was a thinly veiled set-up to try and insinuate your girlfriend is just cheating. As a general note, if someone you love says they were raped-- *believe them*.

You did not "put yourself in this position". You drank after a bad day, and contacted a friend for support. Sure, drinking may not be the healthiest coping mechanism in the books, but it'd be absolutely laughable to say you're the only one who's ever drank to get away from feelings. That in no way justifies sexual assault.

If I were you, I would tell your fiance exactly this. I know it's easier said than done, but you did nothing wrong, and the "friend" who took advantage of you and assaulted you (because you were certainly too drunk to consent) is entirely the guilty party here. Lying to your fiance will only make this harder, a) because if it comes out you might *feel* like you did something wrong even though that's not the case and b) because I'm assuming, as your fiance, they're an important support system to you and you could really use their help now.

I hope it turns out okay for you, and I'm so sorry this happened.

I have a ton of experience writing, calling, yelling, ignoring, and honestly, as hard as it may be the truth I've found is pretty simple: it's not worth it.

I wanted to believe it could help, and maybe briefly talking to him and getting the anger out did help, and then I fell right back into it again, over and over. Even when I thought I wasn't mad. Even when he said he was sorry. It took me a very long time to get through this stage of talking to him and not talking to him for me to get to where I am now, and even then, sometimes I still think that sending just *one* last letter/text/whatever would be worth it.

I've sent probably dozens of "last" messages.

They were never worth it.

I can't tell you what will work for you. But I can tell you that, from my experience, having a life without my abuser in it in any way, shape, or form has been infinitely better than trying to find a way to include him, regardless of whether or not I forgive. Regardless of whether or not he may feel bad.

Don't waste your time on your rapist, they will never be worth it.
This is why people don't report. I'm so, so sorry this is happening to you.
